reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A tremor occurring in a body part that is itself affected by dystonia
Characteristically irregular, jerky and position- or task-dependent, contrasting with the regular rhythm of essential tremor
A null point may exist, being a limb or head position at which the tremor markedly attenuates or disappears
A sensory trick (geste antagoniste) may reduce the tremor, as it does the underlying dystonia
Head and hand tremor are common presentations and are frequently asymmetric
It is distinguished from tremor associated with dystonia, in which the tremulous body part is not itself dystonic
The presence of dystonic posturing is the key feature separating it from essential tremor
reference.pathophysiology: Dystonic tremor is considered a manifestation of the same disordered basal ganglia and cerebello-thalamo-cortical network dysfunction that underlies dystonia, with deficient inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration producing both the sustained abnormal postures and the superimposed oscillation. Its position dependence and its responsiveness to sensory tricks reflect the strong influence of afferent input on this dysfunctional motor control, and help to distinguish it physiologically from essential tremor.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed clinical examination for dystonic posturing, a null point and sensory tricks
Surface electromyography to characterise the tremor pattern where the diagnosis is unclear
DAT imaging to help distinguish from Parkinson's disease when parkinsonism is suspected
MRI brain where a structural or secondary cause is suspected
Copper studies in younger patients to exclude Wilson's disease
Genetic testing where an inherited dystonia syndrome is likely
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or generalising dystonia in a young person suggesting a secondary cause
Abnormal eye movements, hepatic or psychiatric features suggesting Wilson's disease
Distractibility, variability and incongruent features suggesting a functional disorder
Associated parkinsonism or focal deficits pointing to an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Dystonic tremor tends to be chronic and can be difficult to treat, but it is not life-threatening. Focal presentations, particularly head and hand tremor, may respond to botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscles, and some patients benefit from oral medication; refractory, disabling cases may be considered for deep brain stimulation. Overall function is usually preserved with appropriate symptom management.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing dystonic tremor as essential tremor and missing the underlying dystonia
Overlooking a null point or sensory trick that would clarify the diagnosis
Failing to consider Wilson's disease in a younger patient
Expecting a uniform response to standard essential-tremor treatments
